projects.title: Making identity verification easier to get right
projects.summary: Clearer guidance, fewer avoidable verification errors.
projects.subtitle: Clearer guidance, fewer avoidable verification errors.
projects.description: I refined Hijra’s e-KYC journey across several iterations, helping people capture their ID correctly and review the information extracted from it. The work balanced user guidance, verification technology, and compliance requirements.
projects.impact: +16% automated approvals after the final iteration
projects.impactNote: Reported in the original portfolio; measurement scope awaiting confirmation.
projects.role: Product & interaction design · 2022–2024; outcome reviewed February 2025

cover.alt: Making identity verification easier to get right — original portfolio design

body.heading: The challenge
body.text: A low approval rate was pushing registrations into manual review and creating extra work for operations and customer support. The original study describes up to 100 registration and e-KYC support tickets per month. Users often trusted the OCR result without checking their identity details.

image.alt: Original Hijra e-KYC flow

body.heading: 2022: asking people to pause
body.text: The first iteration introduced a five-second review countdown. Usability sessions were encouraging, but launch feedback showed that a timer alone did not make the extracted information clear enough. The original study reports a partially masked improvement of 6.x%; I have not presented it as an exact metric.

image.alt: First iteration of identity data review

body.heading: 2023: making review explicit
body.text: I removed the timer, brought personal details onto the review screen, added a confirmation sheet, and clarified the ID photo frame. The study reports a 13% increase in automated approvals and no user complaints about this flow from Q2 to Q4.

image.alt: Second iteration with data review and confirmation

body.heading: 2024: helping users recover
body.text: Changes to the OCR service introduced new issues, and regulatory constraints limited vendor changes. I redesigned capture guidance for ID photos and selfies, added explicit field confirmation, and made failure feedback and resubmission clearer. Repeated failures moved to manual review after three attempts.

image.alt: Updated photo capture and verification guidance

body.heading: The reported outcome
body.text: The final iteration launched at the end of Q4 2024. By February 2025, the study reports a 16% increase in automated approvals. The overview also cites 35%, but does not explain how the figures relate; the final-iteration result is shown here pending confirmation.

body.heading: What I learned
body.text: People need clear ways to check technology’s output. Improving the journey meant working with product, engineering, operations, and compliance, while recognizing where the verification service itself constrained the experience.

gallery.alt: Help and resubmission screens for identity verification

projects.title: A clearer homepage for everyday banking
projects.summary: Putting useful actions where people can find them.
projects.subtitle: Putting useful actions where people can find them.
projects.description: Hijra’s homepage had grown crowded as teams added competing features and messages. I reshaped its hierarchy to make banking actions, benefits, and relevant services easier to discover.
projects.impactNote: Reported in the original portfolio; measurement scope awaiting confirmation.

cover.alt: A clearer homepage for everyday banking — original portfolio design

body.heading: The challenge
body.text: The homepage had become a collection of competing widgets. Important promotions sat low on the page, oversized components used valuable space, and users did not always understand the benefits available to them.

body.heading: Listening before rearranging
body.text: We interviewed employees and entrepreneurs aged 25–35 with medium to high digital confidence and account balances of up to IDR 5 million. Their feedback pointed to unclear benefits, weak prompts to act, and difficulty finding useful features.

image.alt: Research synthesis and homepage mapping

body.heading: A shared hierarchy
body.text: Cross-functional ideation and four design critique sessions helped align competing priorities. The new structure grouped core banking actions, featured services, campaigns, prayer times, and spiritual wellbeing in a clearer order.

image.alt: Homepage information architecture exploration

body.heading: Making benefits visible
body.text: I kept essential banking actions central and brought relevant campaigns into view earlier. Small interaction cues, including the free-transfer treatment, helped communicate benefits without adding more clutter.

image.alt: Revised Hijra homepage and feature hierarchy

body.heading: The reported outcome
body.text: The detailed study reports a 12% increase in monthly transactional users and an 8% increase in engagement time. The summary instead labels the 8% result as retention, so its definition still needs confirmation. Awareness also improved in follow-up feedback, without a stated numerical result.

body.heading: What I learned
body.text: Good information hierarchy depends on agreement about what matters. Bringing stakeholders into the critique process helped turn competing requests into a more coherent experience.

projects.title: Helping Hijra reach its first 100K users
projects.summary: Finding a reason to join before banking features were ready.
projects.subtitle: Finding a reason to join before banking features were ready.
projects.description: With core banking features still awaiting approval, we explored Islamic lifestyle services that could make Hijra useful from day one. I helped translate user motivations into a product direction the team could build on.
projects.impact: 100,000 users reached — a shared team milestone
projects.impactNote: Reported in the original portfolio; measurement scope awaiting confirmation.

cover.alt: Restored visual of Hijra’s Islamic lifestyle features, based on the original portfolio cover

body.heading: The challenge
body.text: Hijra’s early product had limited banking capabilities while regulatory approval was in progress. Our research showed that people had little reason to register when the features they expected were not yet available.

body.heading: Understanding the audience
body.text: We focused on Muslim adults aged 20–35, including employees, entrepreneurs, and students. Interviews helped us explore which everyday needs the app could support beyond financial transactions.

image.alt: Research and ideation map for Hijra’s early product

body.heading: A broader reason to return
body.text: The direction brought together daily prayers and dhikr, event information and recordings, faith and life guidance, and clearer prayer times. We also refined the Quran reading experience, including the move from Indo-Pak to Uthmani script.

image.alt: Hijra’s recorded Islamic study video interface

body.heading: From ideas to delivery
body.text: Product, design, and business development teams shaped and reviewed the direction together. The features were developed over a quarter, supported by partnerships and programming such as the Halfdeen series.

image.alt: Hijra question and answer service interface

body.heading: The outcome
body.text: The original portfolio reports that Hijra reached its first 100,000 users. This was a shared acquisition milestone supported by product development and partnerships; it should not be attributed to design alone.

body.heading: What I learned
body.text: When the expected product is constrained, research can reveal a different reason for people to use it. The strongest direction connected user motivations with what the team could realistically deliver. Some research details remain confidential.

projects.title: Making fuel depot operations easier to read
projects.summary: A clearer interface for a demanding operational environment.
projects.subtitle: A clearer interface for a demanding operational environment.
projects.description: I redesigned a legacy HMI for Pertamina’s Banjarmasin fuel depot. The focus was on grouping related information, improving visual hierarchy, and making fuel-loading status easier to interpret.
projects.impact: Clearer operational hierarchy and loading feedback

cover.alt: Making fuel depot operations easier to read — original portfolio design

body.heading: The challenge
body.text: The legacy interface used a dated visual style and scattered information. Operators had to work harder to understand the status of fuel-loading activities and the relationships between controls.

image.alt: Original Pertamina fuel depot HMI

body.heading: Designing around the task
body.text: I regrouped related information, reduced visual clutter, and used a dark interface to establish clearer contrast. The redesign emphasized what operators needed to understand and act on during loading.

image.alt: Redesigned Pertamina depot control interface

body.heading: Motion as operational feedback
body.text: The tanker illustration and loading animation made the loading process easier to follow. Motion supported system status rather than serving as decoration.

body.heading: Delivery and limits
body.text: The original portfolio describes a five-day brief and about 12 hours of design production. It does not provide measured usability or engagement results, so this case presents the design rationale rather than a quantified improvement.

body.heading: What I learned
body.text: Operational interfaces benefit from clear relationships between information, controls, and feedback. Their usefulness also depends on maintenance and validation with the people who operate them.

projects.title: A more encouraging financial journey
projects.summary: Making progress visible, one milestone at a time.
projects.subtitle: Making progress visible, one milestone at a time.
projects.description: An exploration of Hijra’s loyalty experience, bringing financial journey levels and achievement feedback into a clearer interface. The concept pairs practical progress with warm, purposeful encouragement.

cover.alt: A more encouraging financial journey — original portfolio design

body.heading: The concept
body.text: The original design introduces financial journey levels: Hijrah, Hamasah, Istiqomah, and Qudwah. Each level explains a stage of progress in ethical banking.

body.heading: Making the next step clear
body.text: The level screen distinguishes completed milestones, the current stage, and the next goal. A progress indicator gives the achievement context rather than treating it as a standalone badge.

body.heading: Celebrating progress
body.text: A dedicated achievement screen recognizes reaching a new level and offers a clear path to the next goal. The language is encouraging and rooted in the values of the product.

body.heading: Scope
body.text: This is an interface exploration in the original portfolio. No research, launch, or performance evidence is provided, so no business impact is claimed.
